source.title: Representation Gap: Explaining the Unreasonable Effectiveness of Neural Networks from a Geometric Perspective
source.authors: David Perera; Victor Moura; Lais Isabelle Alves dos Santos; M. F. C. Haddad; Flavio Figueiredo

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper cites neural scaling laws but does not test or rely on held-out language-model cross-entropy scaling, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or the other listed claim versions. Its own results concern a different quantity: geometric representation gap versus dataset size.
record.gate_note: The paper derives and empirically studies representation-gap scaling with training dataset size, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute. Its empirical results are recorded under fits_no_version; the paper does not test any listed version.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan et al. only as related work. Its own results concern a geometric 'representation gap' versus training-set size. This is measured on tiny diffusion MLPs trained to memorise synthetic manifolds, so it is a different construct from held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute. The n^{-2/d} law is derived from quantization theory, not fitted to a scaling regime, so it does not bear on V5 either.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that the representation gap scales asymptotically as n^{-2/d}, governed by the task's intrinsic dimension. Equivariance reduces d and so provably improves generalization. The derived estimator recovers known dimensions on synthetic data and gives estimates on image datasets consistent with prior estimators. Nothing is concluded about language-model loss scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes geometric representation gap as a function of dataset size rather than measuring language-model loss against model size, token count, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper considers i.i.d. versus optimally diverse dataset sampling and equivariant versus non-equivariant models; these are settings for its representation-gap analysis, not tests of the listed claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: Representation gap of diffusion models trained on optimally diverse synthetic datasets follows the predicted n^{-2/d} law (Hypercube, Wave). Equivariance lowers the effective dimension d, steepening the slope.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For interpolating (equivariant) generative models on data manifolds, the representation gap decays as n^{-2/d}, with d the quotient intrinsic dimension of the task.

record.problems: The measured quantity is representation gap rather than held-out language-model loss, and the experiments shown in Figure 4 use optimally selected datasets. The plotted empirical values are not stated numerically in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version results are omitted. Figure 2 discusses theoretical representation-gap slopes, not empirical language-model loss results.

untested.parts: Held-out language-model loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss in other modalities or regimes. The representation gap of memorising diffusion models on synthetic manifolds is not loss scaling.
Downstream performance versus scale or loss.
Dependence of exponents or allocation on setup and fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: Table 1 (intrinsic-dimension estimates) and Figure 2 (theoretical slopes with an empirically estimated constant) are correctly left out of the rows. They are not claim-bearing. The Figure 4 experiments use optimally selected datasets, and the models are small MLPs; there is no parameter or compute axis.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger language-model runs from smaller runs.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same held-out-loss power law holds across other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices.
